The key idea here is something called transfer learning, which means that we are going to adapt a model already trained to perform a task to a new context using data from that new domain.

Think of it like this: if you already know how to play piano, then learning guitar is easier for you than for someone with no prior musical training, because you already understand things like melody, rhythm, and musical structure. Transfer learning works the same way for AI.

Why 16 chars? Chosen by Notagen authors

16 characters is roughly the length of one meaningful musical unit in ABC notation. short enough that the char-level decoder can reliably reconstruct it, long enough that each patch carries a musically coherent chunk
Why medium?

The real question is whether 1024 is enough to encode a 16-character musical patch into a single vector. Consider that the input is a flattened 2048-dimensional one-hot vector (16 × 128) being projected down to 1024. That's a 2:1 compression. Since the one-hot input is extremely sparse (only 16 of the 2048 values are nonzero), 1024 dimensions is more than sufficient to capture all the information — you're really only encoding 16 character choices, each from a set of 128. Going much smaller (say 256) might start losing the ability to distinguish similar patches; going much larger (say 2048) would add parameters and compute without much benefit since the input itself is so sparse.
Layers? Transformer blocks

Each layer contains a self-attention mechanism and a feed-forward network. More layers means the model can learn more complex, abstract representations. The patch-level decoder has 20 layers because it needs to reason about long-range musical structure (how phrases relate across an entire piece). The char-level decoder only needs 6 layers because its job is simpler — decode one 16-character patch from a single hidden vector.
